Straitly
STRAYT-lee
adverb
From strait (Latin strictus, “drawn tight, narrow”) + -ly; hence strictly, closely, urgently, with binding force. It has no kinship with straight, “not crooked” — a strait is a narrow place, and to charge straitly is to bind narrowly.

Biblical Definition

Straitly means strictly, closely, with a binding tightness — the adverb of a charge that leaves no room to move. It is not our word straight; a strait is a narrow passage, and to be straitly charged is to be hemmed in by the command. Joseph “straitly sworn” his brethren about his bones (Exo 13:19), and four hundred years later Moses carried them out of Egypt: an oath bound that tight outlives the man who took it. Jericho “was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel: none went out, and none came in” (Jos 6:1) — a city sealed as tight as fear could seal it, and the walls fell anyway at the appointed shout. Our Lord uses the word constantly in Mark: cleansing the leper, “he straitly charged him, and forthwith sent him away” (Mar 1:43); and so with the healed blind, and the devils, and the raised child. Christ is no seeker of crowds; He binds men to silence, refusing a fame built on wonders rather than on the cross. The word turns dark in Acts, where the council flings it back at the apostles: “Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name?” (Act 5:28). Here two straitly-charges meet head-on — the Sanhedrin’s and Christ’s — and Peter answers that we ought to obey God rather than men. Every man is straitly charged by someone. The only question is whose narrow command binds him when the two commands cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Strictly; closely; urgently; with binding force — from strait, narrow, not from straight.

expand to see more

STRAITLY, strictly; rigorously; with a close and binding charge.

From strait, Latin strictus, “drawn tight, narrow”; not from straight.

Also closely, narrowly, as a city straitly shut up (Jos 6:1).

Joseph straitly sware the children of Israel concerning his bones (Exo 13:19).

Christ straitly charged the healed to tell no man (Mar 1:43).

Key Scripture

Exo 13:19 — "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you."

Jos 6:1 — "Now Jericho was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel: none went out, and none came in."

Mar 1:43 — "And he straitly charged him, and forthwith sent him away;"

Act 5:28 — "Saying, Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name? and, behold, ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man's blood upon us."

Modern Corruption

A live misuse, and a plain one: the age will be straitly charged by nothing, having reduced God’s binding commands to suggestions and His narrow way to a matter of taste.

expand to see more

There is a real corruption here, and it is not of the word but of the thing. Our generation recognizes no straitly. Commands are heard as preferences, vows as intentions, and the moral law as counsel a man may weigh against his feelings. Joseph straitly sware his brethren, and the oath held its grip on a nation for four hundred years until Moses hoisted the coffin and marched. Christ straitly charged the men He healed, and the charge bound them. But an easy-believism that will confess a Saviour and refuse a Lord has emptied the adverb out of religion altogether: it wants the healing without the charge, the benefit without the binding, and a God whose every word may be renegotiated. A command that binds nothing has commanded nothing.

Two straitly-charges meet in Acts, and every believer will one day stand where they cross. The council said, “Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name?” — and Christ had straitly commanded the very opposite, that repentance and remission be preached in His name among all nations. Peter did not split the difference or seek the middle: we ought to obey God rather than men. The world will always have a straitly of its own, and it grows bolder as the church grows softer. Note also that Jericho was straitly shut up, none going out and none coming in — and the walls fell flat at the appointed shout. No strictness of man can bind what God has purposed to open.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means strictly, closely, with binding force — from strait, narrow.

expand to see more

Straitly — from strait, Latin strictus, “drawn tight, narrow.”

It is no kin to straight; a strait is a narrow place, not an unbent line.

It denotes a charge so close that it leaves no room to move.

Jericho was straitly shut up, and the walls fell anyway (Jos 6:1).

The council straitly commanded silence; Christ straitly commanded preaching.

Usage

"Joseph straitly sware his brethren, and the oath held a nation four hundred years (Exo 13:19)."

"Christ straitly charged the healed leper — He would not build a fame on wonders instead of the cross."

"The council straitly commanded silence; Peter answered that we ought to obey God rather than men."
